strengths: BiAlign presents a clear, relevant contribution to ICL distillation: supplementing token-level alignment with teacher-guided rankings of demonstration subsets. The method requires no additional inference computation.

The main results consistently support the practical effectiveness claim. In Table 1, BiAlign improves average performance over Output-Align from 29.4 to 31.0 with the 13B teacher and from 30.2 to 32.7 with the 70B teacher, improving every evaluated benchmark. Extensions to Llama 3, Phi-3, and Qwen-2.5 strengthen the evidence beyond one model family.

The computational controls are valuable. The paper acknowledges approximately 2.3 times the training FLOPs and compares against Output-Align trained on additional subset data and BiAlign trained for fewer epochs. These comparisons support attributing gains to the training objective rather than simply additional computation or data exposure.

The paper provides substantial supporting analysis, including held-out preference agreement, reverse-KL compatibility, demonstration-selection integration, and sensitivity studies. Public datasets and models, explicit objectives, pseudocode, and core hyperparameters provide a reasonable foundation for reproducing the approach.
weaknesses: The main-conference case is limited by the gap between demonstrated performance improvements and stronger explanatory claims. Increased preference agreement does not establish that BiAlign reproduces the teacher's information-prioritization mechanism. Likewise, Table 2 does not establish greater benefit on harder reasoning tasks: relative gains depend on baseline accuracy, absolute gains are not monotonic with the proposed difficulty ordering, and the comparison excludes Output-Align.

The particular ranking objective needs stronger justification. With distinct teacher ranks and all pairs included, zero loss in Equation 3 requires equally spaced normalized student log-probabilities, a stronger condition than matching ordering. The denominator also needs specified handling for equal or nearly equal scores. Table 5 does not give the exact alternative objective, and comparisons with conventional pairwise ranking losses would clarify the contribution of the proposed formulation.

Several experimental details remain underspecified: the distribution of subset sizes and sampling procedure, exact evaluation prompts, loss reductions, precise checkpoints for the additional model families, and QLoRA settings. No implementation or processed-data release is identified. Table 7 also reports GSM8K's full 8.5K size without clearly identifying the evaluated split and count. These reporting gaps weaken exact reproducibility.

Uncertainty reporting is limited. The three repetitions vary prompts, without reported independent training runs, and the meaning of the ± values is not defined. Most additional experiments report only aggregate means. Consequently, small ablation differences and the modest HumanEval gains on 164 problems warrant more restrained interpretation, although the consistent main-table improvements remain persuasive.
